## Explicit microphone-boundary clock

`lamp_audio::capture::MicrophoneOn::with_clock` takes an owned
`Fn() -> MonoTime` source for the microphone boundary. The existing `new`
constructor and the Linux `Microphone` alias retain the host monotonic
clock. No production call site selects a fixture clock. This is an explicit
library constructor, available to integration fixtures; it is not a runtime
flag, a global override, or a worker clock controller.

The getter must promptly read the current admitted time without advancing
it, waiting, doing I/O or pumping work. Authority snapshots and boundary
read timestamps must use that same domain. The caller owns the clock's
lifetime and updates. Separate microphone instances can own independent
sources. Ordinary construction still validates before sampling and opens
nothing; installing permitted authority still opens nothing.

Every original clock sample remains at its original operation boundary.
The same source supplies construction and authority checks, open/prepare,
start, read and status-observation timestamps. Device status timestamps
remain separate, unchanged, and optional. Clock regression retains the
original permanent boundary fault; it never switches to host time. The
250 ms authority lease, strict read budget (more than 10 ms), partial-buffer
expiry, privacy checks, error precedence, device calls and cleanup are
unchanged. A controlled timestamp is not measured microphone acquisition
or host latency, and a clock getter establishes no completed I/O or exit.

New source tests cover ordinary/explicit-host parity, independent fixed
clocks and driver timestamps, validation before clock access, the exact
10 ms read boundary, authority expiry after actual scripted device calls,
partial expiry across would-block, permanent clock regression, and device
error/expiry/read-budget precedence. They use the same capture boundary
and existing scripted device; only explicit fixture updates move time.
The original tests and their assertions remain unchanged. This preparation
adds no scenario migration or speedup claim.

The capture worker loop, its pacing, the Linux capture-hold Rig, warm-up,
transports and Provider fixtures remain on their existing paths. Clock
admission, completed worker polls and owned thread exit are separate work.
Scripted boundary tests can run on Unix development hosts, but macOS
excludes the ALSA alias and Linux worker integration. Native Linux checks
must compile those callers and exercise the existing capture-hold binary;
its PR-profile exclusion means an ordinary PR-profile pass alone
does not provide that evidence.
